_note: All thresholds for the traffic-light report live here. Numbers marked NASA come from NASA's 2011 non-binding recommendations (NASA-USG Lunar Historic Sites, Rev A). All other numbers are our team's own choices and are explained on the site under 'How it is calculated'.

energy._note: Our choices, not a standard. 14 days is about one lunar day of sunlight, the usual life of a solar-powered lander, so the colour changes with the landing date. The Sun counts only when it is higher than sun_min_elevation_deg: with a very low Sun the shadows are long and the panels collect little. (A 30-day window always covers a whole lunar cycle, so every place came out about 50% sunlit and the check could not tell dates apart.)

communication._note: Our choices, not a standard. Same 14-day window as the energy check. Earth counts when it is above the horizon.

keep_out_km._note: NASA 2011: 2.0 km around lander sites, 0.5 km around impact sites, or 3 sigma of landing uncertainty, whichever is greater. NASA's text covers US sites; we apply the same distances to every site in the list as a precaution (our choice).

neighbors._dust_note: NASA 2011: rocks thrown by the Apollo landers reached up to 1.5 km, and the lunar horizon is about 1.8 km from any point. Dust is not given a distance by NASA; we flag neighbours within twice the horizon distance (2 x 1.8 km = 3.6 km) as 'may be in line of sight on a smooth Moon' (our approximation, no terrain).
neighbors._terrain_note: Only when data/horizons.json has a terrain profile for the point. If the terrain in the direction of a neighbour rises at least this many degrees above the horizontal, we treat gravel and dust risk from that neighbour as shielded (one step lower). This is a rough approximation: the profile tells how high the terrain is, not how far away. The NASA keep-out distance is never lowered by terrain.
